cards.title: Direct Marketing vs. General Advertising: Why the Offer Drives Response
cards.summary: Direct marketers test offers and generate roughly 10x more orders than brand-driven advertising focused on messaging and image.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest effort when a promotion underperforms — messaging polish vs. offer structure
steps: Recognize the core split the source draws: general advertisers concentrate on messaging, image, and brand awareness; direct marketers concentrate on the offer and the action they want the prospect to take.
Treat the offer as what the prospect gets (brochure, sample, trial, discount) combined with what they must do to get it (call, click, return a card).
Replace assumption with testing: direct marketers test lists, media, appeals, headlines, formats, page elements, banner design, and offers rather than relying on focus groups or opinion research.

A Kern Organization study cited by the source found selling the offer instead of the brand produced roughly 10 times more orders and sales in direct mail promoting high-lifetime-value services such as cable, long-distance, and cell phone subscriptions.
Position offers as the highest-leverage lever when a promotion is otherwise competently written, since weak offer mechanics cap results regardless of copy quality.
Use the opening (headline/lead) and the closing (offer and its presentation) as the two highest-leverage zones in promotional copy.
caveats: The 10x figure is one study of specific direct-mail categories with high lifetime value; treat it as an example, not a universal multiplier on all offers.
The source's stance favoring offer-testing over market research is a direct-response philosophy, not a rule that research is worthless everywhere.

cards.title: Lead Generation vs. Order Generation: Two Different Offer Systems
cards.summary: Lead gen is two-step (inquiry then follow-up close), order gen is one-step (promotion produces the sale directly), and offers differ for each.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether a campaign should capture a sales lead or produce a direct purchase
steps: Classify the campaign: order generation (mail order / one-step) asks a stranger to send money in direct response to one promotion; lead generation (two-step) asks for an inquiry first, then follows up to close.
For order-generation campaigns, put the pricing, product, and offer terms in the promotion itself, since no salesperson is available to handle objections after the fact.
For lead-generation campaigns, make the inquiry easy and low friction, then plan staffing and follow-up for the second step.
Accept that offer strategy — selection, planning, testing — can make or break a campaign even when the design and copy are strong.

For ecommerce, a purchase conversion behaves like one-step for low-consideration goods, while high-ticket, configurable, or enterprise-priced products usually need a lead-capture step (quote request, demo, consultation) before the sale.

In the source's copywriter mailing, the writer converted roughly 10–25% of leads from his information-kit letter into sales within six months — a reminder that lead volume and revenue depend on downstream follow-up.
caveats: The 10–25% lead-to-sale conversion is one freelance-services example over a six-month window, not a benchmark for ecommerce.
Lead capture only pays off if there is a realistic follow-up process; otherwise inquiries are waste.

cards.title: Four Offer Types: Soft, Hard, Negative, Deferred
cards.summary: Lead generation has four fundamentally different offer categories, each matching a different prospect-readiness level.
cards.use_when: Designing offer options for a lead-gen or consideration-heavy campaign
steps: Soft offer: prospect requests printed or downloadable material (white paper, catalog, brochure, PDF) using a reply mechanism that requires no personal contact — no phone call, no sales pressure.
Hard offer: prospect must arrange contact with the seller — a phone call, meeting, estimate, demo, or consultation — giving the seller a captive audience to sell to.
Negative offer: reply element asks 'Not interested right now because… (give reason)', disarming prospects and extracting objections.
Deferred offer: reply element says 'Not interested right now. Try us again in (month/year)', capturing future-need timing without triggering immediate follow-up calls.
Match to intent: soft offers suit researchers and cold prospects; hard offers suit serious or urgent buyers; negative and deferred capture non-buyers who still hold signal.
Place the negative or deferred option in the P.S. or end-of-body of the sales letter so it supplements rather than competes with the primary offer.
caveats: Soft offers are sometimes dismissed as 'brochure collectors,' but the source argues soft leads often convert just as well as hard leads.
Negative and deferred options usually draw small response volume; their value is diagnostic and follow-up signal, not raw lead count.

cards.title: Choose Three Offer Options: Soft, Hard, and Negative or Deferred
cards.summary: Most lead-gen promotions should offer two to three response options with one clearly emphasized as primary.
cards.use_when: Building reply elements or landing pages that ask a prospect to take an action
steps: Avoid the common mistake of a single offer option — in most cases include two or three.
Best-practice combination: a soft offer, a hard offer, and either a negative or a deferred option.
At minimum, include both a soft and a hard offer, designating one as primary and the other as secondary.
Make the primary offer the one you emphasize in copy and graphics and the one you hope prospects accept; give the secondary option as a fallback for prospects unwilling to take the primary step.
Example: if you want appointments, the primary can be a free no-obligation consultation; the secondary soft offer appears later (a free special report requested by mailing the reply card).

Add a negative option when testing a new offer or when you expect prospects to have specific reasons for not responding; add a deferred option when significant numbers of prospects likely have future rather than immediate needs.
caveats: In the source's copywriting mailing, over 90% of respondents chose the soft offer and fewer than 10% chose the hard offer — expect a skewed split when you add options.

cards.title: When to Make the Soft Offer Primary
cards.summary: Make free literature or information the primary offer when brochures, specs, or catalogs are the normal first step in your buyer's process.
cards.use_when: Deciding offer priority for complex, technical, high-explanation products or buyers who resist talking to sales
steps: Choose a soft primary offer when a brochure, catalog, or data sheet is the standard first step in your industry and skipping it would be counterproductive.
Choose it when prospects would be reluctant to meet or phone you and a literature offer gives them a low-risk reason to respond.
Choose it when the product is complex and requires standardized written explanation — as with industrial equipment sold to engineers and purchasing agents who need technical detail before deciding.
Choose it when you lack phone coverage staff and your operation is built around mailing a standardized inquiry-fulfillment package.
Choose it when prospects are geographically far from reps or there are no regional offices to call on them.
Choose it when you already have a proven fulfillment kit that screens out unqualified prospects and sells effectively to qualified ones.
caveats: A strong existing kit is the operative qualifier — a weak brochure as a soft offer mostly generates unqualified inquiries.
The source describes industrial manufacturers as typical soft-primary marketers; this is a pattern, not a prescription for every technical product.

cards.title: When to Make the Hard Offer Primary
cards.summary: Make phone or face-to-face contact the primary offer when your salespeople close better on inbound calls or when print cannot convey the product.
cards.use_when: Deciding offer priority for simple services, unique or demo-driven products, or audiences that don't read
steps: Choose a hard primary offer when you prefer inbound phone inquiries because your salespeople close better on hot calls than on mailed leads.
Choose it when sending printed material just delays the sale, or when there is little information to convey and a two-minute call can do the job.
Choose it when you have a free trial or nominal-fee trial that prospects will accept if you can sell them on the phone or in person.
Choose it when your product is unique or difficult to describe in print and is better shown via phone or demonstration.
Choose it when your audience is not readers or information seekers at all.
Illustration from the source: an adult vocational training marketer found that offering a brochure was a waste — prospects had to attend a free introductory class in person for the program to sell.
caveats: The vocational-training example is one marketer's discovered rule for their market; it does not mean brochures never work in education.
Hard offers shrink response volume, so weigh lead count against lead quality for your sales capacity.

cards.title: Diagnose Weak Response With a Negative Offer
cards.summary: A negative offer option captures why prospects aren't responding, which separates bad copy from bad product-market fit and sometimes surfaces prime prospects.
cards.use_when: Testing a new product, service, or offer in direct mail or a new channel where a null result would be uninterpretable
steps: Add a reply-box line reading 'Not interested right now because: (Please give reason — thank you.)' and reference it in the P.S. or body of the letter.
Use it specifically when testing a new product, service, or offer, so that a low response can be attributed to the market rather than to the mailing piece.
Interpret returned reasons as diagnosis: price too high, incompatible technology, wrong product type, or no need — each implies a different fix.
Increase response by giving a logical reason to reply, e.g. 'Even if you are not interested, complete and return the card so we can give your free [offer] to another person on our list.'
Treat responders who explain their non-interest as follow-up candidates: they have framed a specific objection that a skilled salesperson can overcome.
Recognize the sales advantage: the hardest prospect to sell is the unreachable one who never responds and never says why.
caveats: The source notes the negative option only increases overall response slightly — its main value is diagnostic and objection-surfacing.
Do not use the negative option as a substitute for adequate sample size; a single mailing's reasons are anecdotal.

cards.title: Capture Future Buyers With a Deferred Offer
cards.summary: A 'Try us again in (month/year)' option captures prospects who have future needs but avoid the soft offer to dodge follow-up calls.
cards.use_when: Selling products or services that are bought on a future trigger date — contract renewals, budget cycles, planned purchases
steps: Add a reply element reading 'Not interested right now. Try us again in (month/year)' to your reply card or landing page.

Understand the psychology: some prospects avoid checking the soft-offer box because they fear immediate follow-up calls they don't want yet. The deferred box lets them declare future interest without inviting current pressure.
Choose deferred over negative when you believe a significant number of prospects will need your service at some future date rather than right away.
Choose negative over deferred when testing a new offer or when you suspect many prospects won't respond for specific reasons you want to learn.

Honor the timing: the source describes at least two cases where prospects who checked 'Try us again' turned out to have specific projects with specific start dates; immediate literature plus a phone call at the requested time produced sales.
caveats: Deferred-option response is infrequent; the source could not provide statistical results because mailing volume was too low.
Failure to actually follow up at the requested time wastes the option entirely.

cards.title: Bait Pieces: Free Content That Can Double Lead Response
cards.summary: Offering free, genuinely useful content as the reason to respond can roughly double lead-generation response rates and still convert well.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer for a lead-generation campaign, email, ad, or direct-mail piece
steps: Define the bait piece: free information offered to generate inquiries, deliberately designed to hook a response that sales can follow up.
Confirm the content is relevant, valuable, desirable, and specific to the prospect's needs — not a disguised brochure.
Expect roughly a doubling of response versus the same copy without the free content offer; the source calls the free booklet offer a mistake to omit for most lead-generation marketers.

Understand why it works: information seekers respond to free advice; a free offer interrupts skimming because readers stop to see what they can get; and people respond to free things even when they aren't excited about them.
Emphasize the offer in copy and graphics — the sample reply card in the source headlines the free white paper and pictures the white paper, not the product.
Expect 10–35% or more of bait-piece requesters to eventually do business with you, depending on product and cost.
caveats: The doubling claim and the 10–35% conversion range are the author's experience across promotions, not guaranteed figures.
Bait pieces only lift response when the topic actually interests the reader; a generic topic adds cost without hooking anyone.

cards.title: Pick the Bait Piece Topic and Title
cards.summary: Choose a narrow topic that interests the reader while subtly favoring your product, then title it with 'how to' or numbered-list formats.
cards.use_when: Planning a free booklet, white paper, special report, or tip sheet for a lead-gen offer
steps: Pick a topic that serves the reader's self-interest while helping sell your system, product, or approach — the balance is the reader's benefit against your promotion.

Adopt Michael Stelzner's 'silver bullet': include a section on how to select or what to look for when buying the type of product you sell. Keep it editorially neutral in tone, but ensure your product satisfies every criterion listed.
Check topic relevance by audience: a small-business owner would ignore 'How IBM Designs and Codes Its Software Systems' but respond to 'How to Choose the Right Software for Your Business.'
Title with 'how to' phrasing or numbered formats ('7 Ways,' '6 Steps,' '14 Winning Methods') to create curiosity and specificity.

Prefer a narrow, targeted topic over a broad one so you can cover it in convincing detail — the source cites Fala's 'Should I Personalize? A Direct Marketer's Guide to Personalized Direct Mail' as effective precisely because it zeroes in on one topic.

Recall IBM's example: a 200-page free paperback on evaluating business software, written as if it would sell for $20, positioned IBM as having 'written the book' while its software matched the checklist.
caveats: The IBM book required substantial ghostwriting investment; not every offer justifies book-length content.
Manipulative checklists that only your product passes can damage credibility if prospects detect the slant.

cards.title: Choose the Bait Piece Format and Media
cards.summary: Match format to effort and perceived value: tip sheets are cheap, booklets and reports are standard, books and binders raise perceived value.
cards.use_when: Deciding what physical or digital form a free content offer should take
steps: Fact/tip sheet: desktop-published or typeset on one or two sides of a single 8.5x11 sheet; 500 single-sided copies run roughly $30–$50; print on yellow, gold, or bright stock to raise perceived value over white.

Address the cheap look of tip sheets by producing them as larger posters on better framing-suitable stock — the source cites a consulting firm that promoted writing seminars with one-page posters on grammar and usage topics.
Booklet: folded or saddle-stitched, page sizes of 4x9 inches to fit a #10 envelope or 5.5x8.5 inches for a 6x9 envelope; more detailed than a tip sheet, less than a book.
Special report: full 8.5x11 pages mailed in a 9x12 envelope or delivered as an immediate PDF download; photocopy or offset, collate, and bind in a clear plastic cover.
Tailor one report to multiple audiences by keeping the body identical and swapping only the introduction and front cover.

Raise perceived value for 50+ page documents by putting pages in a three-ring binder and calling it a manual; avoid printing the cover directly on binders so dated content doesn't strand inventory — use a title page or a trap-in sleeve.

Consider self-published paperbacks for proven content: expect a 500-copy minimum and better pricing at 2,000–3,000 copies; quote only short-run printers (under 5,000 copies), as general printers charge 2–3x.
For small niches, use print-on-demand to print one copy at a time, accepting several times higher per-copy cost.
caveats: POD per-copy cost is many times a short-run printer's, so it only makes sense for small, uncertain demand.
The source's cost figures date from the 2009 publication era; verify current printing and duplication prices.

cards.title: Price the Bait Piece on Its Cover
cards.summary: Putting a credible cover price on free content raises perceived value, lets you charge non-prospects, and validates the price in your copy.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a free booklet, report, manual, or book that you intend to give away as an offer
steps: Print a price in the upper right-hand corner of the cover even though the piece is given away free.

Use it for three purposes: raising perceived value (a $29 item free beats a free item free), justifying paid copies for non-prospects such as students or brochure collectors, and gracefully charging the occasional person requesting multiple copies for a seminar or class.
Set credible price ranges: $1–$2 for a tip sheet, $3–$10 for a booklet, $7–$29 for a special report by length, $15–$25 for a book, and $15–$25 for a manual.
Avoid overpricing — if the cover price is too high, prospects conclude the price exists only to inflate the offer.
Legitimize the price by posting bait pieces on a website page where visitors can order them at full cover price through a shopping cart, so the stated price is real.
Accept that sales from this page are incidental; the purpose is to back the price claim in your offer copy, not to build an information-product business.
caveats: The source's suggested prices and his own reports library reflect an earlier era and specific market; recalibrate for current expectations.
A cover price your own site never honors invites skepticism if prospects check.

cards.title: Write Bait Piece Content That Sells Subtly
cards.summary: The body of a free booklet must be pure information that delivers on its headline, with all selling confined to covers and back matter.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing the content of a free lead-generation booklet, report, or white paper
steps: Deliver on the headline's promise: useful, accurate information the reader can apply.
Do not demand novelty — many readers read to affirm what they already know; repeating known material while framing it clearly still earns expert status. Add one or two genuinely new ideas if you can.
Keep the body free of your advertising message; turning the booklet into a sales pitch angers readers who expected advice.

Confine promotion to the back pages after the main text, and use the front and back covers: list your firm as author with address and phone on the front, and add a fuller 'About the Author'-style company description and next step on the back.
Calibrate depth so the reader gets interested in hiring you or buying your product, but don't give away so much that they no longer need you.
Choose length by format: a full-length book requires much more detail than a one-page tip sheet.
caveats: The 'don't give away too much' guidance is the source's judgment and can conflict with generous content strategies that build trust; the balance depends on the offer's purpose.
Excessive back-page promotion can undercut the credibility built by the body.

cards.title: Label Premiums to Change Perceived Value
cards.summary: How you name and describe the same free item materially changes how desirable it appears and how prospects respond.
cards.use_when: Writing offer copy that describes a free premium, report, or gift
steps: Accept the principle stated by Bob Hemmings: the same offer stated differently is perceived as a uniquely different offer and can substantially boost results.
Choose benefit-laden labels over literal ones: 'consumer awareness guide' rather than 'brochure,' 'executive briefing' rather than 'white paper.'

Use the American Spectator example as the model: a saddle-stitched reprint of past Clinton articles was offered as 'The Bill & Hillary Clinton Inside the White House Report' — far stronger than describing it as ripping old articles out of back issues and stapling them.
Ensure the relabeled item still delivers on the name; the label raises response, but the content converts.
Apply the same relabeling discipline in ecommerce to naming free gifts, bonus guides, or bundled extras.
caveats: Labels that overpromise relative to the contents create disappointed respondents and can hurt follow-up conversion.
This is a copy and perception technique, not a method for misrepresenting what the prospect receives.

cards.title: Use Audio CDs and DVDs as Higher-Value Bait Pieces
cards.summary: Non-print bait pieces can stand out in a crowded inbox, survive screening, and keep your contact visible for longer.
cards.use_when: Considering media beyond print or PDF for a lead-generation offer, especially B2B
steps: Weigh the structural advantages: CDs and DVDs are less common than print and PDF, stand out among paper, often bypass the secretary who screens and discards paper mail, and are unlikely to be thrown away.
Assume recipients will either consume the content, route it to the right person, or at minimum keep it in a desk drawer where your company name and phone number stay visible.
Favor audio CDs for easy, low-cost production: record a live presentation, edit in a studio, and ship as the bait piece.
Dismiss the assumption that shorter is better — the source has succeeded with 30-to-90-minute audio CDs when the content is purely useful information, less for 10–20-minute pieces.
Capitalize on listenability: prospects can play audio while driving, exercising, or doing chores, while video demands dedicated attention.

Estimate costs from the source: recording a presentation by a professional with equipment costs $200–$400 plus expenses, studio editing runs $75–$95 per hour for under half a day, and duplication with a laser-printed label in a vinyl case or sleeve costs about $1.25 per unit.
caveats: Cost and production figures date from the 2009 publication and should be re-quoted.
Video requires far higher production effort than audio, and the source does not treat them as equally easy options.

cards.title: Offer Mechanics: Value Stacking, Payment Fractioning, and Value Assignment
cards.summary: Mechanics like stacked bonuses, per-day price framing, and priced free premiums change how prospects evaluate an offer's terms.
cards.use_when: Restructuring the terms of an offer to raise conversion without changing the price
steps: Stack perceived value against the asking price — the source lists this among the growth-level offer mechanics, alongside premium bait pieces and guarantees.
Use payment fractioning to shrink the mental size of a lump sum: express a $297 annual fee as 'just 81 cents a day' or split it into four quarterly payments of $39.
Use drop-in-the-bucket framing for recurring or lump-sum prices so the number reads as small relative to the value exchanged.
Assign a distinct dollar value to a free premium (e.g., $29 printed on the cover) and validate it by actually selling that item at that price elsewhere.
Apply these mechanics selectively; they alter how terms are perceived, not the underlying offer's economics.
caveats: The source itself classifies these as growth-side, advanced mechanics — baseline offers with clear pricing and standard guarantees are the prerequisite.
Per-day framing and installments can mislead if the total cost or financing terms are obscured; keep the full price disclosed.
No numeric lift figures are given for these mechanics in this section.

cards.title: The Unfair Advantage Guarantee and Deferred-Payment Structures
cards.summary: High-conversion guarantee and payment structures for zero-marginal-cost goods and B2B continuity offers.
cards.use_when: Designing guarantee terms for digital products or payment terms for B2B continuity programs
steps: Consider the 'Unfair Advantage' guarantee: give a full refund while explicitly telling the buyer to keep the delivered product. The source reports this dramatically lifts initial conversion and notes it is especially effective for digital goods with near-zero marginal cost.
For B2B continuity programs, consider a modified bill-me offer: send an invoice, but withhold the product — or the premium — until payment clears.
Weigh the marginal cost of the retained product against the conversion lift before adopting the keep-it guarantee; for physical goods with real unit costs, the economics differ from digital goods.
Treat standard unconditional guarantees and basic pricing clarity as the baseline layer, and these complex structures as growth-side options to test.
caveats: The source's effectiveness claims for the Unfair Advantage guarantee are directional; no numeric lift is stated in this section.
Keep-it guarantees on physical products can be exploited and carry real unit-cost exposure.
Bill-me with withheld product can create friction and chargeback disputes — verify local billing and consumer-protection rules before adopting.

OceanofPDF.com Introduction What Albert Einstein Can Teach You About Improving Your Advertising Results _____________________________ “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up.” — Mark Joyner _____________________________ I assume you are a small-business owner, marketing manager, Internet marketer, direct marketer, ad agency creative director, copywriter, product manager, advertising manager, or any other marketer concerned with generating leads and orders, and not just communicating brand messages. In this book, we will explore ways to dramatically improve response rates to your promotions anywhere from 10 percent to as much as 900 percent — just by creating and testing different offers. As you know, an “offer” is simply what your prospects get when they respond to your ad or mailing — combined with what they have to do to get it. In its simplest form, an offer might be “Call us toll-free for a free booklet on adjustable beds.” The booklet is what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. “Give your reader something to do and make it easy for him to do it,” writes G. Lynn Sumner in his book How I Learned the Secrets of Success in Advertising (North Audley Media). “Tell him where to get what you have to sell, how much it costs — and why he should do it now.” An irresistible offer promises prospects something so compelling or desirable that they can’t help but call, write, or go online to get it. “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up,” writes Internet marketing pioneer Mark Joyner. Or, to paraphrase Marlon Brando in The Godfather, it’s an offer your prospect can’t refuse. What’s the biggest difference between general advertising and direct marketing? In my view, it’s that direct marketers recognize the critical importance of the offer, while general marketers, by and large, do not. More than that, direct marketers focus their efforts on driving the largest volume of qualified prospects to accept their offers. General advertisers spend their time agonizing over the messaging in their ads and finding creative ways to express it. General advertisers are concerned with image and brand. What image of the company does their advertising convey? Are consumers aware of their brand and what it stands for? What brand messages do they want to communicate? How can they make those brand messages memorable? Direct marketers focus on presenting compelling reasons why consumers should buy their products right then and there, as well as overcoming any objections the consumers may have. They are concerned with the action they want the consumer to take — and how to get him or her to take it. General advertisers sit in conference rooms, brainstorm what they want to say about the product, and then spend large amounts of money communicating those messages in their advertising. They often ask consumers for their opinions of products, brands, and advertising through focus groups, surveys, and other market research. Direct marketers do not assume they know what consumers want to hear or what will sell best. They test everything: lists, media, key sales appeals, headlines, envelope teasers, direct-mail package size, mailing formats, Web page colors, banner designs, and offers. Many direct marketers eschew market research in favor of live tests of actual promotions, believing the only opinion expressed by consumers that has any meaning is the one they vote on with their checkbooks and credit cards. So which approach is better — the brand-driven approach of the general advertiser or the offer-driven approach of the direct marketer? A recent study by The Kern Organization found that when marketing sells the offer instead of the brand, it generates approximately 10 times more orders and sales: (Source: Target Marketing, 4/08) Figures are based on direct mail promotions to sell offers with high lifetime customer values including cable TV subscriptions, long-distance and cell phone service. The wisdom of stressing the offer in advertisements has been known for well over a century. In 1902, three years before he wrote his groundbreaking paper on the theory of relativity, a young Albert Einstein ran newspaper ads offering his services as a tutor in math and physics. The ads prominently offered a “free trial lesson” — showing that free offers really are a smart marketing tactic! The two areas in your promotional copy where you can get the most leverage — the greatest lift in responses and orders — are the opening and the closing. The opening is mainly the headline and lead of your copy, as well as its graphic design and presentation. In his book The Architecture of Persuasion, Michael Masterson shows you how to write compelling headlines and leads. The closing of your copy is largely the offer and its presentation. In How to Create Irresistible Offers, I’ll show you how to craft strong offers that make your marketing make more money for you. I do have one favor to ask. If you’ve used a great offer that works, why not send the promotion to me so I can share it with readers of the next edition of this book? I also welcome your comments and questions on How to Create Irresistible Offers. You can reach me at: Bob Bly Copywriter / Consultant 590 Delcina Drive River Vale, NJ 07675 Phone: (201) 505-9451 Fax: (201) 573-4094 E-mail: rwbly@bly.com Web: www.bly.com OceanofPDF.com 1 Offers That Bring in a Flood of New Leads There are two major categories of direct marketing: lead generation and order generation. Order generation, also called “mail order,” seeks to generate an order for a product directly from the promotion. Mail order is “one-step marketing,” because you make the sale in a single step. As Bill Bonner of Agora Publishing describes it, “You send strangers a letter, and they send you money.” Lead generation seeks to produce an inquiry or sales lead — to get qualified prospects to metaphorically raise their hands and say, “Hey, I might be interested in this product. Tell me more.” Lead generation is “twostep marketing.” The first step is sending the promotion and generating the inquiry. The next step is following up on the inquiry and closing the sale. Strong offers are critical to the success of both lead generation and mail order marketing. The strategic planning, selection, and testing of offers can make or break a campaign, regardless of how well designed or well written the piece is. In this chapter, we’ll look at the offers that work best for lead generation. Creating a Simple Offer That Works A typical offer for a lead-generating promotion might be “Call us tollfree for a free catalog on adjustable beds plus a copy of our free booklet: How to Get a Good Night’s Sleep.” The catalog and booklet are what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. As a rule, the more valuable and risk-free the offer seems to the reader, the better your response. The presentation of the offer — the copy used to describe it, the graphics, its position in the promotion — is also important. Usually, the more you emphasize and stress the offer in copy and graphics, the higher your response rate. Another rule of thumb: The clearer and more understandable your offer, the better your response. The lack of a clear, distinct offer can significantly depress response. The simplest, most popular offer in lead generation is probably the offer of a brochure describing the product or service. In direct mail, this typically reads: “For a free brochure on the Widget 2000, complete and mail the enclosed reply card today.” What the prospects get is a brochure describing the product. What they have to do to get it is fill in and mail a reply card. The offer of a free brochure can and does work for numerous products and services. However, you can often come up with a much more attractive offer — one that will get many more people to be interested in your proposition and respond to your ad or mailing. In lead generation, there are four fundamentally different types of offers: soft, hard, negative, and deferred. Get More Leads With a Soft Offer In a soft offer, the prospect requests some type of printed material that is mailed or shipped to him or downloaded online as a PDF document. The prospect makes this request by using a reply card or other response mechanism that does not require face-to-face or other personal communication between him and the seller. For example: For a FREE copy of our white paper on Best Software Audit Practices, complete and mail the reply card today. Want our latest catalog? Call toll-free 800-XXXXXXX. We’ll rush a copy first-class as soon as we hear from you. To download our new free white paper, “Calculating ROI From ERP Implementation,” click here now. The important thing to note about the soft offer is that it’s the most painless, risk-free way for the prospect to raise his hand, get in touch with you, and say, “I may be interested — tell me more” … without having to subject himself to sales pressure of any kind. The typical soft offer in a direct-mail letter reads as follows: “If you’re interested in learning more about what Product X can do for you, just complete and mail the enclosed reply card for a free brochure.” The prospect checks off a box on a reply card and mails it to you. You mail the requested literature back. The prospect has expressed interest, responded, and received information without making personal contact. The soft offer appeals to prospects who do not have an immediate need and are “just looking,” and to those who have an immediate need but want to gather preliminary information without speaking to agents or sales reps. The soft offer generates a high level of response, because there is no sales pressure or risk of being pitched by high-pressure sales types. It promises details that can be reviewed by the prospects at their leisure. Many marketers mistakenly believe that all people who respond to soft offers are just collecting brochures or white papers, and are therefore not real prospects. For this reason, they avoid soft offers. They say, “If the prospect doesn’t pick up the phone and call me, she’s not really interested. I don’t want to waste time and money sending her expensive color brochures that she’s just going to file or throw away.” While there’s some validity to this point of view, it usually turns out not to be true. Soft leads can be extremely profitable, and often the conversion rate is just as good as it is with hard leads. In a survey of IT professionals, for instance, 57 percent said that white papers influenced their buying decisions. For most promotions, the best strategy is actually to give the reader a choice of several offers, not just a soft offer or a hard offer. Target Your Best Prospects With Hard Offers The opposite of the soft offer is the hard offer. A hard offer in lead generation requires or results in face-to-face or other personal contact between buyer and seller. Whether in person or on the phone, the seller has the prospect “captive” for purposes of doing some selling. In the hard offer, the prospect typically calls or writes the advertiser to arrange a meeting, demonstration, initial consultation, or appointment. There is direct person-to-person contact between buyer and seller — initially over the telephone and, usually, later face to face. During these contacts, outbound telemarketing representatives or salespeople attempt to persuade prospects to buy the product or service being offered. Examples of hard offers: * To get a no-obligation estimate for adding a new family room or den to your house, just complete and return the Free Estimate Request Form enclosed. * For a free analysis of what you’ll need to save to put your children through college, call XXX-XXX-XXXX today. The hard offer is ideal for prospects who have a serious interest, an immediate need, or a desire to buy something fairly soon and want to sit down and talk with vendors. The prospect responding to a hard offer, especially if doing it by telephone, typically feels a fairly urgent need to gather more information for an immediate or upcoming purchase. With a hard offer, the prospect is taking a definite (if tentative or uncommitted) step toward purchasing the product. A soft offer, by comparison, gets more of a “Let me look you over” or “We’ll wait and see” response. Turn a “No” Into a “Maybe” With a Negative Offer In addition to soft and hard offers, there are two other basic categories of offers: negative and deferred. The negative offer reads as follows on the reply element: Not interested right now because: (Please give reason — thank you.) Typically, reference to the negative offer is made in the P.S. or elsewhere in the body of the sales letter, using the following language: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card. Thank you. The negative offer provides a response option for people who qualify as prospects — that is, they have a need or problem your product addresses — but, for whatever reason, are not ready to take the next step in the buying process: getting more information on your product. A negative offer instructs the reader to respond even if she does not want to learn more about your product, which is disarming and unusual. By using a negative offer option, you can often get a response from a small portion of your prospects. That response can be increased by giving the reader a logical reason to reply: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card so we can give your free [whatever is being offered] to another person on our list. Thank you. The negative offer should be used when you are testing a mailing on a new product, service, or offer you haven’t promoted before using direct mail. The reason you use the negative offer is that, without it, if you get a low or no response to your mailing, you don’t know whether it’s the mailing piece that’s ineffective or the product, service, or offer that isn’t right for the market. With the negative option, people will tell you why they are not interested in your offer. Perhaps the price is too high. Or your technology is not compatible with the systems they are already using. Or they don’t like your type of product or don’t use it. This information not only helps you readjust your marketing plans, it demonstrates that the mailing was unsuccessful for reasons other than ineffective copy and design — something that’s good to know if you’re the person who wrote or designed it. A second benefit of the negative option is that it can slightly increase your overall response rate. You might object and say, “But all the people who check the negative option box have told us they are not prospects.” But quite the opposite is often true: If people take the time to tell you why your offer isn’t right for them, they may be prime prospects. They’re telling you they have some sort of need, but your product as described in the mailing doesn’t seem quite right … and that they want you to get back to them with a product, service, or offer that is right for them. Actually, your product or service may be ideal for them, but your ad or mail copy may not have communicated that effectively — or they misunderstood or didn’t read carefully enough. That’s okay. By completing the negative offer option box, your prospects have set themselves up for follow-up and closing by a skilled salesperson. If you have ever been a salesperson, you know the most difficult prospect to sell is the one you can’t reach — the one who never responds to your letters, never returns your phone calls, or says he is not interested but won’t say why. A prospect who fills in the blank space on your reply card where it says “Please give a reason why you are not interested” has framed a specific objection, which can be overcome with the proper selling argument. Try us again in (month/year) The deferred offer encourages responses from prospects who do not have an immediate need but may have a future requirement for your product or service. Some of these prospects won’t check off the soft offer option box (“[ ] Please send me a brochure”) because they think, “If I check off this box, they’re going to follow up with a phone call and pester me. I don’t have a need right now.” The deferred offer option box says to this prospect, “If you have no immediate requirement but may have a future need, you can use this box to let us know that you have a future need, without getting calls and annoying follow-up from salespeople now.” When do you use the negative as opposed to the deferred offer option? Use the negative offer when you are testing a new offer or when you think many prospects might not respond for specific reasons. Use the deferred offer when you think a significant number of prospects might need your services at some future date rather than right away. Increase the Odds of Sales Success With Multiple Offer Options A common mistake in lead-generating promotions is to have only one offer option. In most instances, you should have two or three options. In lead generation, the best results usually come from having three offers: a soft offer, a hard offer, and either a negative or a deferred offer. At minimum, you should have both a soft and a hard offer, with one of the two being primary and the other secondary. The primary offer is the one you hope your prospects will respond to and the one you emphasize in your copy and graphics. For example, if you want a face-to-face meeting with your prospects, you would urge them to call and arrange an appointment. A “free, no-obligation initial appointment” would be your primary offer, the one you stress in your letter or e-mail. The secondary offer is included to give those prospects who will not take you up on your primary offer a second reason to respond. If a prospect is not willing or ready to take you up on your offer of a free initial meeting, introduce the secondary soft offer at the end of your ad or letter copy. (“P.S. Again, don’t forget to put a cover price on the book. About $10 to $15 for a slim paperback seems right. 7. You have selected the topic, title, and format. Now it is time to determine the contents, make an outline, and write the copy for your booklet or report. The most important thing to keep in mind when writing informational premiums like free booklets or reports is that the contents must deliver on the promise of the headline, convey useful information helpful to the reader, and be accurate. It is not necessary for the contents to be revolutionary or give the reader all new information. Many people read to affirm current beliefs or reinforce existing knowledge. So if your booklet mostly repeats what they already know, they’ll be happy with it. More important, they’ll think you’re a wise, knowledgeable expert on the topic. However, if you can give the reader one or two genuinely new ideas or things they may not have thought of before, so much the better. It will make your booklet or report even more valuable to them. Do not include your advertising message in the body of the booklet. The contents should be pure information. You promised the reader knowledge; you impress the reader by conveying that knowledge. If you turn the booklet into a sales pitch, the people who sent for it expecting helpful advice will be angry, disappointed, turned off, and not inclined to do business with you. You can insert an ad or promotional copy on the pages in the back of the book, at the end of the regular text. How much information should be included in your bait piece? It depends on the length and format. A full-length book, for example, must obviously provide more detail than a one-page tip sheet. As a rule, make your booklet or report helpful and fascinating, but don’t overdo the detail. You want to tell the prospect enough to get her interested in hiring you to solve a problem. You don’t want to tell so much in your report that it eliminates the need for the prospect to hire your firm or buy your product. If the body is pure information, can you do any selling in the booklet? Yes, but keep it low key. On the front cover, under the title, put your firm as the author, giving the address and phone number. Repeat this information on the back cover, adding a more complete description of your company, your product or service, how you can help the reader, and the next step she should take to learn more about your product or service. This should read like the “About the Author” bios you find on how-to books written by business experts, giving enough information to whet the reader’s appetite without being blatantly sales-oriented. Increase Perceived Value With an Electronic Bait Piece One way to generate additional interest and make your bait piece stand out even more is to offer your information in the form of an audiocassette, audio CD, DVD, or software CD-ROM. One advantage of these formats is that they are not as widely used as print and downloadable PDF files. Therefore, they are a bit unusual and likely to attract more attention. Also, CDs and DVDs tend to stand out in an in-basket crowded with paper. Other advantages? CDs and DVDs usually get past secretaries who screen and throw away lots of paper mail. Because a CD or DVD has a higher perceived value than paper and is a tangible object, it won’t get thrown away. Experience has shown that prospects will take the time to listen to or view the audio CD or video, or at least make sure it gets passed on to the right person within the organization. Printed pieces are not treated with the same degree of importance. Finally, even if the prospects don’t immediately listen to or view the tape or disk, they will probably keep it in a desk drawer rather than throw it away. So every time they open the drawer, they will see the tape or disk imprinted with your company name and phone number. Audio CDs Sell Your Products to Prospects While They Drive Audio CDs are the easiest and least costly audiovisual medium to use as information bait pieces. Some marketers using audio CDs think that briefer is better and limit the message to 10 or 20 minutes. But if the audio contains pure, useful information, it can be much longer. I have been successful promoting both my seminars and my consulting and copywriting services using audio CDs that are 30 to 90 minutes long. Prospects must set aside valuable time to watch a DVD. But they can listen to your audio CD while driving the car, exercising, or doing household chores. Audio CDs do not require the high level of production that videos do.
